Hasted
HAY-sted
verb (past tense)
The Authorized Version’s past tense of haste, from the Old French haste, speed, urgency. It renders the Hebrew mahar, to hurry, and chush, to make speed — the outward sign of an inward reckoning that the matter will not wait.

Biblical Definition

Scripture is careful about who hasted and why, for haste is a moral index. Abraham, seeing three strangers at his tent door, “hasted to dress it” (Gen 18:7) — the hospitality of a man who reckons the guest more urgent than his own ease. Rebekah at the well “hasted, and let down her pitcher” (Gen 24:18) and again “hasted, and emptied her pitcher into the trough” (Gen 24:20), and this readiness to serve a stranger and water his camels is the very sign the servant had asked God to give. The bride of Isaac is identified by her speed in serving. Against these stands another haste altogether: “Haman hasted to his house mourning, and having his head covered” (Est 6:12) — the hurry of a proud man fleeing a humiliation he cannot undo. And the taskmasters hasted the people (Exo 5:13), which is haste imposed by tyranny, the driver’s whip rather than the servant’s love. The lesson is plain enough. Haste is not a virtue in itself; it takes its character from its object. To be swift in duty and slow to wrath is godliness; to be swift in sin and slow in mercy is the mark of a corrupt heart. What a man hurries toward tells you what he loves.

Webster 1828 Definition

Made haste; hurried; moved or acted with speed. In Scripture, the outward evidence of what a man reckons urgent, and so a test of his affections.

expand to see more

HASTE, v.i. To move with speed or celerity; to hurry.

HASTED, pp. and past tense of haste, the AV’s regular form.

To urge or drive forward with speed; as, the taskmasters hasted them (Exo 5:13).

From the Old French haste; allied to the Saxon haest, violence, vehemence.

Rendering the Hebrew mahar, to hurry, and chush, to make speed.

Key Scripture

Gen 18:7 — "And Abraham ran unto the herd, and fetcht a calf tender and good, and gave it unto a young man; and he hasted to dress it."

Gen 24:18 — "And she said, Drink, my lord: and she hasted, and let down her pitcher upon her hand, and gave him drink."

Exo 5:13 — "And the taskmasters hasted them, saying, Fulfil your works, your daily tasks, as when there was straw."

Est 6:12 — "And Mordecai came again to the king's gate. But Haman hasted to his house mourning, and having his head covered."

Modern Corruption

Our age treats speed itself as a virtue and slowness as a defect, which inverts the biblical rule — Scripture commends haste in duty and mercy, and condemns haste in judgment, in speech, and in the getting of wealth.

expand to see more

The corruption is the worship of velocity. Modern life measures a man by his output per hour and calls hurry productivity, so that a settled, unhurried spirit looks like laziness and a frantic one looks like diligence. Scripture makes a sharper distinction. It commands haste toward obedience — I made haste, and delayed not to keep thy commandments — and toward mercy, as Abraham and Rebekah show. But it forbids haste in exactly the places the modern world demands it: he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly, he that hasteth to be rich shall not be innocent, and he that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him. The world has the categories precisely reversed. It hurries into judgment, into speech, into debt, and into wealth, and then complains of exhaustion.

Recover the plain sense: ask not how fast but toward what. Abraham ran to the herd for a stranger; Rebekah ran to the trough for a servant’s camels; Haman ran home to hide his face. The same speed serves love in one man and pride in another. Cultivate the haste of Gen 18:7 — swift to feed, to serve, to forgive, to obey — and cultivate the slowness the Apostle James commands, slow to speak and slow to wrath. A Christian who is quick where God bids him be quick and slow where God bids him be slow will look strange to the age and will keep his soul.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old French haste, speed — the outward measure of what a man counts urgent, and therefore of what he loves.

expand to see more

Hasted — AV past tense of haste; Old French haste, urgency.

Hebrew mahar, to hurry (Gen 18:7; Gen 24:18).

Transitive sense: to drive another with speed (Exo 5:13, the taskmasters).

Commended toward duty and mercy; condemned toward wrath, speech, and riches.

Rebekah’s haste is the sign by which the bride is identified (Gen 24:18–20).

Usage

"Gen 24:18–20: Rebekah is marked out as the chosen bride by her readiness to serve."

"Exo 5:13 shows haste imposed by tyranny — the driver’s haste, not the servant’s."

"Est 6:12: Haman’s haste is flight from shame, the exact opposite of Abraham’s."
